items.content:
The latest CIPS Procurement & Supply Salary Guide 2026 makes for an interesting read.

A few findings stood out:

- 61% of procurement and supply professionals received a salary increase.
- The average increase was 7.4%, comfortably ahead of global inflation.
- Australia reports the highest average procurement salary (c.US$110,000), followed by Europe (c.US$92,000), Canada (c.US$84,000), New Zealand (c.US$82,000) and the UK (c.US$76,000).

Taken together, the findings suggest that procurement continues to be a profession where skills and experience are recognised and rewarded.

Two thoughts for future editions:

- With the Statement of Work (SoW) market continuing to grow (around 20% CAGR), it would also be interesting to understand how procurement professionals are participating in that market. The report notes that only 4% of respondents currently work as interims, but a future survey could also explore how many are working through consultancies or agencies delivering services under SoW arrangements.
- It would be valuable to broaden the geographical coverage to include the USA, Central and South America. ISM cover the US market, but there could be real value in a more joined-up global perspective between CIPS and ISM.

I look forward to seeing how the guide develops in future editions.

#Procurement #SupplyChain #FutureOfWork #StatementOfWork #WorkforceStrategy

items.content:
The more I try to get my head around AI, the less convinced I am by the “jobpocalypse” narrative applies to procurement and supply chain.

John Burn-Murdoch in the Financial Times recently referenced the Jevons paradox. When technology makes something more efficient, we often end up using more of it, not less. My favourite example is LED lights. They dramatically reduced the cost of lighting, which led to an explosion in overall use and ultimately wiped out a significant portion of the intended savings. I just need to look at my kitchen ceiling to know it’s true.

I think procurement and supply chain could experience the same effect.
AI will reduce the cost of sourcing, forecasting, optimisation and supplier analysis. But after COVID exposed the fragility of global supply chains, and with continued geopolitical uncertainty in Eastern Europe and the Middle East, organisations are demanding more resilience, optionality, and scenario planning, not less.

That probably means:
• more sourcing to align with the market 
• more suppliers and greater diversity 
• more multi-sourcing strategies to mitigate risk 
• more product variation to align with demand 
• more live data to enable real-time decision making

To manage these additional demands and the evolving AI landscape, entirely new roles will emerge. A couple of months ago, I shared Gartner’s view that new roles will include Business Ontologists, AI Product Managers, Agentic AI Portfolio Managers and Procurement Business Architects.

Historically, firms simplified operations because complexity was expensive. AI may fundamentally change that equation. The future of procurement may not be smaller teams. It may be teams managing far greater complexity than was previously possible. Procurement may be heading for its own lighting moment.
Not a few bulbs in the centre of the room but thousands of LEDs illuminating every corner of the supply chain.

items.content:
Like many people, I’ve been trying to get my head around AI in procurement. A post by Asmaa Gad this week really helped. Her Agentic AI Platforms Map (65 platforms, 10 categories, 2026 edition) brilliantly illustrates how crowded this space has become.

Given the number of platforms and categories, I wanted to step back and understand what they actually do. The discussion that followed provided the answer. AI platforms can broadly be viewed as operating across three layers:
- Orchestration: automating end-to-end procurement workflows (e.g. major Source-to-Pay suites such as Coupa, SAP Ariba, GEP)
- Domain Intelligence: generating insight within specific areas—spend analytics (Sievo, Rosslyn), contract intelligence (Icertis, Ironclad), supplier risk (Resilinc, Prewave)
- Data Access: the foundational layer—connectivity, supplier data, and infrastructure that everything else depends on (Palantir, E2open, One Network)

It’s worth noting that the major S2P platforms are increasingly bundling spend analytics and risk monitoring into their core offerings. So are these truly three distinct categories, or three overlapping capabilities? Perhaps the more useful question isn’t “which platform category do I need?” but “which capability will deliver the greatest improvement in performance?” For most teams, it’s the intelligence layer. The workflows already exist—genuinely understanding what you’re spending, with whom, and at what risk is where AI could close the gap first.

items.content:
Non-tech company research can be a useful antidote to AI hype. PwC’s latest AI performance study is a good example, while PwC clearly has an interest in AI adoption, the report is written for buyers and builders of AI in large organisations, not by AI labs thinking about the next round of funding. The study finds that the most "AI-fit" companies deliver 7.2x higher AI driven financial performance than the rest.

The report opens with a familiar scene: a room full of people, a PowerPoint presentation packed with AI pilots, and plenty of questions on deployment, scaling, and business cases. But very few answers.

The report goes on to describe "AI-fitness" as the ability to point AI at what matters, build fit-for-purpose foundations, and embed AI throughout the enterprise, quantified through a nine-category index covering strategy, governance, data, technology and more. Data and technology, for example, is described as "the degree to which a business has modern, scalable platforms and trusted varied data sources accessible to everyone". 

Anyone who completed the London Marathon a fortnight ago knows fitness is built over months and years, not in a weekend bootcamp. AI is the same, anyone expecting to become AI fit overnight is setting themselves up for disappointment, without targeted, sustained effort, rooms full of AI pilots and too little measurable impact will persist.

My favourite part of the report is the ideas in motion section (case studies by any other name). John Deere’s "See & Spray", really gets into the weeds (pun intended), showing how AI can create new revenue opportunities while delivering tangible environmental benefits, not just prettier dashboards.

For anyone interested in or already deploying AI, this report is well worth a careful read (see comments for the link).

- First-order impacts: increased energy and input costs, delays, and volatility.
- Second-order impacts: wider inflationary pressure, supplier instability, and demand uncertainty.
This reinforces the need to focus not just on cost, but on risk, resilience, and scenario planning.

items.content:
AI adoption in procurement is accelerating, largely bottom-up, while governance struggles to keep pace. The gap between adoption and oversight is widening.

Anthropic’s release of Claude Mythos Preview this month is a clear example. It identified thousands of zero-day vulnerabilities, many critical, across major operating systems and browsers. It was Anthropic, not governments, regulators or industry bodies, that highlighted the risks and limited its availability.

At the same time, signals from the market are accelerating adoption. 2026 redundancy announcements across major tech firms include Oracle (up to 30,000 roles or ~18%), Amazon (~16,000 roles), and Meta (more than 8,000 roles) send a clear message that AI is replacing people. Loganix’s 2026 B2B AI Buying Behavior Analysis shows 73% of B2B buyers, including many in procurement, are already using AI tools.

The combination of limited governance and pressure to use AI is driving behaviour organisations may not see, or would not permit if they did. In procurement, this includes drafting RFPs using sensitive data, analysing confidential supplier pricing, providing feedback to suppliers as part of the negotiation process and making evaluation recommendations using approved tools like Copilot without appropriate governance, or shadow AI such as ChatGPT and Claude without approval.

I hope the “Mythos moment” is the point when governments, regulators, and boards come together to define clearer guardrails for AI use.

items.content:
World Sustainable Procurement Day 2026 has just wrapped up.

Hosted by the Sustainable Procurement Pledge (SPP), this year's community event featured 26 sessions delivered back to back over 24 hours. I was fortunate to attend 9 of them, and came away genuinely energised by the quality of organisation, the calibre of presenters, and the depth of content available.

I really wanted to know more about best practice and identify organisations that have moved beyond strategy into measurable delivery.

In summary, here's what best practice looks like:

• Start with the data. Consider all options, including short-term wins such as transitioning to renewable energy, alongside longer-term transformation goals

• Engage broadly. Across your business and your supply base. Listen actively, and be willing to adapt

• Be targeted. Start small, bank early wins, refine your approach, then scale. Momentum matters more than perfection

The sessions that stood out for clearly demonstrating delivery — not just ambition — came from some specific sectors: Pfizer, AstraZeneca, Haleon and Takeda in pharma; Schneider Electric in electrical infrastructure; and Tetra Pak in packaging.

Want to hear it for yourself? SPP will be publishing all 26 sessions across their channels, including YouTube (see comments for the link), over the coming weeks. I'd encourage anyone with an interest in sustainable procurement to take a look.

items.content:
The crisis in the Middle East is already sending ripple effects through global supply chains. For procurement and supply chain leaders, the question is less what’s happening and more how quickly to adapt.
• Energy prices rising
Around 20% of global oil passes through the Strait of Hormuz and refinery disruptions are pushing fuel prices higher. Petrol prices have increased by approximately $0.27 to $3.25 per gallon in the United States, and €0.33 to nearly €2.00 per litre in the Eurozone. Natural gas prices have risen by about $0.15 to $3.02 per MMBtu in the US, while Eurozone prices have surged by roughly €6.08 to €15.58 per MMBtu.
Action: Review fuel hedging, diversify energy sources, and ensure contracts include price adjustment mechanisms.
• Shipping costs and lead times increasing
Last week, shipping a 40ft container (FEU) from the Far East to Europe via the Strait of Hormuz (Suez Canal route) cost approximately $2,844–$3,000. Current reroutes around the Cape of Good Hope have pushed costs to $7,000–$8,500 per container, adding 10–14 days transit.
Action: Secure alternative carrier capacity, negotiate risk-sharing clauses, and review buffer stock for critical SKUs.
• Raw material exposure
Metal, petrochemicals and fertiliser supply is threatened (although it is too early to tell if the rise in fertiliser prices will translate to higher prices on supermarket shelves).
Action: Dual-source away from high-risk regions and map supplier dependencies at least two tiers deep.
• Air freight volatility
Global capacity of air cargo has reduced by a fifth leading to increases in rates, for example, rates from China to US have increased by 15% and South Asia to Europe by 3%. This puts pressure on electronics, pharmaceuticals, and automotive components supply chains.
Action: Prioritise air freight for revenue-critical items and reassess safety stock levels.
• Third party risk management
Margin pressure and disruption may increase supplier insolvency risk.
Action: Run financial health checks on top 20 suppliers; activate dual-source strategies; review contracts, especially force majeure clauses.
For procurement leaders, this is a reminder that geopolitics is now a core supply chain variable.
#Procurement #SupplyChain #RiskManagement

items.content:
Gartner recently shared some interesting analysis on AI's impact on procurement teams. The headline finding? 28% of procurement's time could be automated.

While most procurement professionals recognise a significant proportion of purchase orders are repeats and some parts of the sourcing process could be automated, it's helpful to understand the scale. 

The analysis goes further. Gartner predicts that AI has the potential to reshape 20% of procurement roles by 2030. It's worth noting that with all new technology, organisations that deploy AI without investing in change management (including support for AI literacy and role redesign) won't realise the ROI. So organisations have to invest, not only tools but people, in order to realise the return.

Gartner identifies 4 emerging roles that don't exist in most organisations today:

→ Business Ontologists (ensuring AI reflects real-world sourcing logic)
→ AI Product Managers (optimising procurement AI performance)
→ Agentic AI Portfolio Managers (governing autonomous AI agents)
→ Procurement Business Architects (designing AI-enabled strategies)

What's an ontologist? It's the architect who ensure AI "understands" your reality. (I had to look it up).

Procurement's future isn't about replacing people with AI, it's about redesigning roles to capture AI's strategic value.

Are you preparing your team for these roles, or just thinking you should deploy the technology?

#AI #FutureOfWork #ProcurementTransformation

items.content:
If someone told you buying AI was like buying a cake, it might sound like an April Fool’s joke. Well, Jensen Huang of NVIDIA described AI not as a single tool, but as a “five-layer cake”.

For most procurement professionals, the focus is on the AI models and applications, but for the AI labs like Anthropic and the hyperscalers like Google, the supply chain in more complicated. The cake, or AI stack, includes:
- energy (e.g. Constellation Energy providing energy from nuclear reactors through long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs))
- compute (e.g. NVIDIA’s H100 GPUs are currently the industry standard for large-scale AI training and inference)
- cloud infrastructure (e.g. Amazon Web Services’ Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) is one of the industry-standard, foundational service for cloud computing)
- AI models (e.g. Anthropic’s Claude model is often favoured for coding, creative writing and nuanced reasoning)
- applications (e.g. Cursor provides AI-native Integrated Development Environment (IDE) is a software application that provides an interface for developers to write, edit, test, and debug code efficiently)

Making a cake requires many ingredients as well as a variety of skills. Procuring the AI stack is no different. It involves multiple categories of spend, and a range of capabilities, from category management and strategic sourcing to procurement operations. In this respect, procurement is required to orchestration an entire ecosystem.

Like all categories of spend, procurement benefit from understanding not only the risk from first tier suppliers but the risk from second tier suppliers.
Perhaps not quite an April Fool’s joke after all, and definitely not as simple as it first sounds.

#Procurement #SupplyChain #AI

items.content:
Deloitte published a piece on the agentic supply chain worth reading if you’re in manufacturing or supply chain.

A few things that stood out:
• Agents support a more continuous planning approach through sensing, decision-making, and response instead of waiting on traditional planning cycles.
• This isn’t one agent doing everything. It’s layered across cross-functional, domain, and task-level agents working together across the flow.
• Dropping agents into existing workflows may miss the mark. Redesigning workflows around what humans and agents each do well provides more benefit.
• Humans still own oversight, judgment, and decision thresholds. Agents operate within those boundaries. Governance is treated as foundational, not something added later.

Deloitte also cited Gartner’s projection that ~50% of supply chain management solutions will include agentic AI by 2030. I can see this happening.

Lately I’ve been using Claude to run some simple agents with anonymized data. Things like checking planning data (lead times, purchase order dates, safety stock, etc.), flagging errors, and suggesting corrections based on defined rules or analysis. I’ve also been using it to run existing Python scripts against historical demand and generate forecast recommendations across different models for comparison and approval.

It’s still early, though the shift is noticeable from a productivity standpoint.

Curious how much value is showing up in practice for others?

#SupplyChain #AI

items.content:
When exceptions become the operating model, you don’t notice it right away.

Expedites stop feeling temporary. Overrides feel normal. Workarounds become “how we get things done.”

No one plans for it. It usually starts with a legitimate issue. A disruption. A miss. A customer escalation.

The team adjusts. Then adjusts again. Over time, the workaround sticks. What was meant to be temporary becomes routine.

The issue isn’t that exceptions exist. Every business has them.

The issue is when structure gives way to constant correction.

At that point, performance depends more on effort than structure.

More energy goes in. Stability doesn’t improve. Predictability starts to decline. When predictability declines, performance eventually stalls, even if activity increases.

One simple signal: if the standard process is hard to clearly describe, it may already be gone.

The real question isn’t whether you have exceptions.

It's this: how would you know if they’ve become your default way of working?

#SupplyChainLeadership

items.content:
BCG’s “Supply Chain Planning 2026: Why AI Alone Isn’t Enough” provides a useful reality check on where planning organizations stand. The firm surveyed 181 planning leaders in Q4 2025, and 91% say planning is well represented or fully embodied in overall strategy.

The pressure points show up clearly in the results.

Externally, leaders cite:
• Demand volatility (70%)
• Geopolitics (64%)
• Supply volatility (62%)

Internally:
• Forecast inaccuracy and misalignment (78%)
• End-to-end visibility (38%)
• System limitations (35%)

Most organizations have already invested in APS, though the report notes that many deployments underdeliver when operating models, governance, and data discipline do not evolve alongside the technology.

The maturity story is mixed. Many rate their processes as intermediate or advanced, yet gaps remain in transformation capability and change readiness, financial integration, and data, digital, and analytics.

On AI, realized value today is concentrated in practical areas such as dashboards and reporting, master data management, supply planning and scheduling, and inventory optimization. Agentic AI and GenAI sit at 10% for delivered value so far, and many organizations are still defining roadmaps and integration approaches.

Technology can expand planning capability. Whether that translates into better outcomes depends heavily on how well organizations align assumptions, accountability, and execution.

How closely do these internal and external pressures align with what others are seeing?

#SupplyChainPlanning

(Image source: BCG, Supply Chain Planning 2026: Why AI Alone Isn’t Enough)

items.content:
Last week at MODEX2026 I sat in on a few sessions, and there was a lot of discussion around AI in supply chain.

A few points kept coming up across sessions and with different people:

1.) A lot of the value from AI isn’t being realized because it’s being introduced without a clear problem to solve or a defined use case.

2.) Layering AI on top of existing processes without rethinking how the work should actually be done is leading to stalled or underwhelming implementations.

3.) While some platforms include data cleansing capabilities, there is still hesitation around relying on those outputs. In some cases, the recommendations aren’t accurate enough to build trust.

Start with the problem and the value you’re trying to create. Work backwards through the impact and requirements, and make sure the process and data foundation can support it. The technology follows from there.

#SupplyChain #AI

items.content:
Supply chain data integrity becomes a priority when something breaks.

A cleanup gets launched. Parameters are corrected. Master data is aligned. Systems run better.

Then attention shifts.

A few months later, the same issues resurface.

Lead times don’t match supplier performance. Lot sizes and Minimum Order Quantities haven’t been revisited. Safety stock hasn’t been recalibrated. Overrides increase. New products introduced are missing required planning fields.

Frustration builds. “The system never works” becomes the narrative. Teams revert to old habits. Cross-functional trust weakens.

The problem usually isn’t the cleanup itself.
It’s that the structure to sustain it was never defined.

In practice, it comes down to four things:
𝟭. 𝗚𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗰𝘆 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗹
Define who has authority over planning logic and structural rules.
𝟮. 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝘀𝘁𝗲𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗱𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽
Assign accountability for keeping those inputs current within the agreed rules.
Governance defines the rule. Stewardship maintains within it.
𝟯. 𝗥𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗿𝗲𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄 𝗰𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲
Monitor material drift through normal operating forums and exception management, not a one-off project.
𝟰. 𝗣𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗸𝗮𝗴𝗲
Connect data integrity to service, inventory performance, and cost.

One-time cleanups improve accuracy temporarily.
Operating discipline sustains trust.

If teams stop trusting the system, they will plan outside it and rebuild the very workarounds the cleanup was meant to eliminate.

#SupplyChain #SupplyChainPlanning #DataGovernance

items.content:
In supply chain transformations, I’ve often found that a hybrid delivery approach works better than committing to either Waterfall or Agile.

Certain parts of a transformation benefit from a more predictive structure (Waterfall), while others work better with a more adaptive approach (Agile). That’s why many large programs end up blending the two.

From experience, I’ve seen transformations struggle when they lean too far in either direction. That said, the method chosen really depends on the type of work being done.

If everything is too rigid and structured, parts of the solution may already be outdated by the time they roll out. If everything stays too loose, the work can drift, scope creep sets in, and the program never really stabilizes.

The transformations that delivered the most value and adoption had both program discipline and the ability to adapt as the work took shape inside the business.

A hybrid approach helps maintain the structure needed to move the program forward while still allowing flexibility and value to show up along the way.

Have you found Waterfall, Agile, or hybrid more effective in supply chain transformations?

#SupplyChainTransformation #ProgramManagement
